claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The operculum sits on the upper surface of the foot and acts as a trapdoor that closes the opening when the animal withdraws. Its most essential function is to stop the snail drying out; where it seals fully it also protects against predators.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The inhalant siphon is a tube-like extension of the mantle that draws water into the mantle cavity and over the gill for breathing. It carries chemoreceptors that "smell" or "taste" the water to hunt for food.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The mantle is the body wall that covers the visceral mass. Its skin secretes calcium carbonate and conchiolin to build the shell. In cowries the living animal often partly or fully covers its glossy shell with the mantle.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The queen conch has a long snout, two eyestalks with well-developed eyes, extra sensory tentacles, a strong foot and a sickle-shaped operculum. It browses algae and plant material in seagrass beds and scavenges decaying plant matter.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The queen conch moves by leaping: it digs the point of its sickle-shaped operculum into the sand, then extends the foot and throws the shell forward. Only the front third of the foot touches the ground, and leaping may stop predators following a continuous scent trail.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The flared lip is absent in juveniles and grows once the conch reaches reproductive age; the thicker the lip, the older the conch. Its body's visceral hump stays inside the shell and holds the internal organs.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The siphuncle empties water from new chambers as the shell grows: the animal makes the blood in it saltier, water leaves the chamber by osmosis, and gases diffuse in. It is passive, not pumping.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: A nautilus has 50 to over 90 tentacles of three kinds. Ocular tentacles beside the eyes are sensory; digital and labial tentacles ring the mouth. They have no suckers, yet the digital tentacles grip with an adhesive from ridges on their surface and let go by contracting.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: To swim, a nautilus draws water into and out of its living chamber with its funnel (hyponome), by jet propulsion, which has proved efficient compared with other jet-propelled animals like squid and jellyfish.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: A hermit crab's abdomen is soft and not hardened by calcium, so it must occupy a shell made by another animal or be defenceless; almost 800 species carry such mobile shelters, most often snail shells.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: Moon snails (naticids) plough through sand hunting bivalves and other prey, leaving countersunk bore-holes in the shells they drill.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The radula, often compared to a tongue, is a ribbon of tiny teeth that scrapes or cuts food before it is swallowed.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: Gastropods typically have a well-defined head with two or four sensory tentacles bearing eyes, and a foot positioned below the guts, which gives them their name ("stomach-foot"); like most molluscs they move on this single muscular foot. Many smell through receptors in the skin of their tentacles.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: Sea snails crawl on their foot: its muscles contract in waves that run along it and deform a thin layer of mucus beneath. The mucus lowers friction and seals the gaps under the foot, so it grips and slides at once.
claims.evidenceNote: Describes land and sea snails generally; not measured for the species shown.

claims.text: Once a veliger has settled and metamorphosed, the young snail moves about on the seabed with its foot.
claims.evidenceNote: General description of gastropod veligers.

claims.text: In the related cowrie Mauritia arabica, larvae ready to settle swam less and spread their velum less often, then spent more time on the bottom. They began crawling about 60 days after hatching and metamorphosed, losing the velum, at about 70 days.
claims.evidenceNote: Laboratory observations; in the same study tiger cowrie larvae did not settle, so this comes from a different cowrie.

claims.text: Young queen conch usually stay buried in the sediment for their first year of life.
claims.evidenceNote: Tertiary source summarising the species' life cycle.

claims.text: Queen conch do not crawl slowly along leaving slime trails. They hop: the foot pushes against the bottom and propels the shell up and forward. A study tracked 42 adults with loggers that record when each one is hopping or staying still.
claims.evidenceNote: From a press release on a peer-reviewed study and an encyclopedia account; the paper itself was not read.

claims.text: A nautilus squirts water through its funnel (hyponome) to thrust itself backwards and to make turns. It can swim head first or shell first; the faster it goes, the more efficient shell-first swimming becomes.
claims.evidenceNote: Government species profile and a laboratory study of swimming nautiluses.

claims.text: Nautiluses tracked at Osprey Reef in the Coral Sea spent the day resting at about 200 m or foraging below about 490 m, and the night moving continually between about 100 m and more than 700 m.
claims.evidenceNote: One tracked population; the study notes that nautiluses at Palau were deeper by day.

claims.text: Unlike the adult, a gastropod veliger has two ciliated, semicircular lobes resembling fins or wings, together called the velum, its main means of propulsion and of collecting food particles. The planktonic larval stage can carry it far from the adults that produced it; the velum and foot can be pulled into the shell to protect them, and the velum is lost at metamorphosis.
claims.evidenceNote: General description of gastropod veligers; the shape and size drawn here are illustrative, not of a particular species.

claims.text: Veligers have a band of long compound cilia in front of the mouth (the prototroch), a band of shorter cilia behind it (the metatroch), and a food groove between them whose cilia beat toward the mouth. The long cilia drive the water current; particles are caught between the two opposed bands and passed along the food groove to the mouth.
claims.evidenceNote: A peer-reviewed review of ciliary feeding; it also notes that how exactly particles are caught (the 'catch-up' idea, filmed in veligers by Strathmann & Leise, 1979) is a hypothesis.

claims.text: Each place's water colour, the colour cast on everything in it and its sand are matched to underwater photographs taken there, from Wikimedia Commons: the median colour of open water in each photo, the average colour of the whole frame, and pale sand where it shows. Only colour statistics are used; places with few usable photos borrow from places with the same kind of reef. The list of photos, authors and licences for every place is in data/place-colours.json.
claims.evidenceNote: Photos vary with camera, lens, depth, light and editing, so these are a typical look, not a measurement of the water. Photos lit by a flash or taken out of the water were left out (data/research/place-photo-exclusions.json and the script's filters).

claims.text: Bivalves (class Bivalvia) are molluscs whose soft body is enclosed in two hinged shell halves called valves. The class includes clams, mussels, oysters, scallops and cockles; most are filter feeders.
claims.evidenceNote: Class-level statement. The app has no 'class' scope, so 'family' is used to mean 'its wider group' rather than this species alone. MarineBio and Wikipedia agree; UCMP adds that most bivalves are suspension feeders. WoRMS confirms the class name.

claims.text: Chitons (class Polyplacophora) are marine molluscs whose shell is divided into eight overlapping plates, bordered by a girdle. They use a muscular foot to cling to rocks and other hard surfaces.
claims.evidenceNote: Class-level statement. The app has no 'class' scope, so 'family' is used to mean 'its wider group' rather than this species alone. All three descriptive sources agree on the eight plates, girdle and clinging foot.

claims.text: Tusk shells (class Scaphopoda) are marine molluscs with a tubular, tusk-shaped shell that is open at both ends. They burrow into sediment with their foot and catch food with thread-like tentacles called captacula.
claims.evidenceNote: Class-level statement. The app has no 'class' scope, so 'family' is used to mean 'its wider group' rather than this species alone. 'Open at both ends' is from UCMP and Wikipedia; the rest is in all three.

claims.text: Monoplacophorans (class Monoplacophora) are small deep-sea molluscs with a single cap-like shell. The class was known only from fossils and thought to be extinct until living animals were found in 1952.
claims.evidenceNote: Class-level statement. The app has no 'class' scope, so 'family' is used to mean 'its wider group' rather than this species alone. MarineBio says living specimens were found in the 1950s; UCMP and Wikipedia give 1952.

claims.text: A bivalve's two valves are joined along a hinge by a flexible ligament, usually with interlocking teeth. Adductor muscles pull the valves shut and the ligament springs them open when the muscles relax. Many bivalves pump water in and out through siphons, and their gills (ctenidia) are used both to breathe and to filter food. Bivalves have no head and no radula.
claims.evidenceNote: Class-level statement. The app has no 'class' scope, so 'family' is used to mean 'its wider group' rather than this species alone. Read from the article lead and its 'Muscles and ligaments' and feeding sections. Giant clams fit this plan; NOAA's status review also describes T. gigas siphons, gills (demibranchs) and adductor muscle.

claims.text: A chiton's shell is eight articulated plates (valves) set in a tough muscular girdle that may carry spines, scales or hairs. Most of the body underneath is a large muscular foot, with a row of small gills along each side. The mouth holds a radula whose teeth are capped with magnetite, an iron mineral, and are used to scrape algae from rock.
claims.evidenceNote: Class-level statement. The app has no 'class' scope, so 'family' is used to mean 'its wider group' rather than this species alone. Varney et al. (peer-reviewed) give the aragonite plates and magnetite-capped teeth; UCMP and Wikipedia give the girdle, foot and gills.

claims.text: A tusk shell's shell is a tapering tube open at both ends, with the mantle forming a tube inside it. A muscular foot digs from the wide end, thread-like captacula gather food, and a large radula grinds it. There are no eyes and no gills.
claims.evidenceNote: Class-level statement. The app has no 'class' scope, so 'family' is used to mean 'its wider group' rather than this species alone. Both sources state the absence of eyes and gills; Wikipedia notes the scaphopod radula is the largest relative to body size of any mollusc.

claims.text: A monoplacophoran has a single cap-like shell over a round muscular foot, a poorly defined head without eyes, and a mouth with a radula. Three to six pairs of gills sit in a groove along each side of the foot, and kidneys and muscles are repeated in series.
claims.evidenceNote: Class-level statement. The app has no 'class' scope, so 'family' is used to mean 'its wider group' rather than this species alone. Wikipedia gives three to six gill pairs; UCMP gives five or six (fewer in very tiny species). Neopilina galatheae has five pairs (see neopilina-serial-organs).

claims.text: The true giant clam is Tridacna gigas (Linnaeus, 1758), an accepted species in the World Register of Marine Species (AphiaID 207670), in the cockle family Cardiidae, class Bivalvia.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS REST record read directly; NOAA's classification also lists family Cardiidae, genus Tridacna, species gigas.

claims.text: Tridacna gigas is the largest giant clam and the largest living bivalve. Its shell can reach 137 cm long and the animal over 225 kg, but it is most commonly found at about 80 cm long. NOAA's species page gives a length of up to 51 inches.
claims.evidenceNote: 137 cm = 1,370 mm (maximum) and about 80 cm = 800 mm (most common size), as stated in NOAA's status review; WoRMS lists the same two lengths from the FAO guide. 51 inches is about 1,295 mm.

claims.text: Tridacna gigas lives in shallow tropical Indo-Pacific waters from Myanmar to Kiribati and from Japan's Ryukyu Islands to Queensland. It lives on coral reefs, including atoll lagoons and fringing reefs, among hard corals, on reef rock or on sand and coral rubble. The Great Barrier Reef still has large stocks; it is now rare in the Philippines, Solomon Islands, Marshall Islands and Palau, and locally extinct in Fiji.
claims.evidenceNote: Range, habitat and country status ('frequent', 'rare', 'reintroduced') are from NOAA's status review section 4.4; ADW adds that it is usually embedded in sand or coral rubble on reef flats and lagoons. Old reports from Madagascar and Mauritius are unconfirmed, and East African records are Pleistocene fossils.

claims.text: Tridacna gigas is typically found between about 2 and 20 m deep (NOAA's species page says 6 to 65 feet).
claims.evidenceNote: 6-65 feet is about 2-20 m. ADW and Wikipedia also say usually within 20 m of the surface.

claims.text: A thick, heavy, off-white shell with four to six deep radial folds ending in large triangular points along the opening, often overgrown with corals and worm tubes; the inside is porcelain-white. The mantle is yellowish-brown to olive-green with many small, brilliant blue-green rings. Adults cannot close the shell completely.
claims.evidenceNote: Shell and mantle description from NOAA's status review (citing Rosewater 1965 and others) and NOAA's species page. ADW says 4 to 5 projections and that fully grown clams cannot completely close the shell.

claims.text: Giant clams farm single-celled algae (zooxanthellae) in narrow tubes in the upper layers of the mantle. By day the clam opens and spreads its mantle so the algae get sunlight to photosynthesise, and the algae pass sugars and amino acids to the clam, supplying most of the carbon it needs. In some T. gigas they supply about 90% of the carbon used, and the clam dies if kept in the dark.
claims.evidenceNote: The status review (section 3.5.1) describes where the algae live and what they provide; ADW gives the 90% figure and death in darkness; Wikipedia and the Great Barrier Reef Foundation describe the daytime opening.

claims.text: Tridacna gigas also filters plankton from seawater with its gills. This matters most while small: clams about 4 cm long can get up to 65% of the carbon they need this way, 16-17 cm clams about a third, and large adults can probably meet their needs from their algae alone.
claims.evidenceNote: Figures from the status review section 4.4.1.4 (citing Klumpp et al. 1992); ADW confirms filter feeding on phytoplankton and zooplankton with the gills.

claims.text: Giant clam larvae swim, then settle; juveniles crawl on a foot and later attach with byssal threads. Large species lose the byssus as adults and are held in place by their size and weight: adult T. gigas are free-living and permanently sessile.
claims.evidenceNote: Juvenile byssal attachment and its loss in large species are from the status review section 2.3 (all giant clams); 'lack of byssal attachment (free-living)' for T. gigas is from its section 4.4.1.1; ADW says adults are permanently sessile.

claims.text: Tridacna gigas is a hermaphrodite that spawns sperm and eggs into the water; one spawning releases about 500 million eggs on average. Fertilised eggs, about 0.09-0.13 mm across, become swimming trochophore larvae within 12-24 hours. Spawning may follow the moon; in Australia it is limited to a short summer season, while in Palau it can happen year-round.
claims.evidenceNote: Egg size (90-130 µm) and the 12-24 hour hatching time are from the status review section 2.3 (giant clams generally); fecundity and seasonality are T. gigas-specific (section 4.4.1.3). Wikipedia gives about 12 hours and eggs of 100 µm. 12-24 hours = 0.5-1 day.

claims.text: Within 36-48 hours giant clam larvae become shelled, swimming veligers that feed on microalgae. Over several days they grow a foot (pediveliger), generally 6-14 days after fertilisation (some up to 29 days), then turn into juveniles at about 0.2 mm. Fewer than 1% of fertilised T. gigas eggs are estimated to survive larval development.
claims.evidenceNote: Stages are described for giant clams generally (section 2.3); the report repeatedly gives a pelagic larval duration of about 6-14 days. The survival estimate is T. gigas-specific (section 4.4.1.3).

claims.text: Tridacna gigas grows faster than any other giant clam, typically 8-12 cm a year, slowing with age. Cultured clams in the Philippines grew up to 9.1 mm a month. Shell growth continues throughout life.
claims.evidenceNote: From the status review sections 2.3 and 4.4.1.3. Wikipedia similarly reports laboratory growth of 12 cm a year.

claims.text: Tridacna gigas reaches male maturity at around 6 years of age and female maturity by 9-10 years, later than most other giant clams.
claims.evidenceNote: Status review section 4.4.1.3, citing Gomez & Mingoa-Licuanan (2006). Giant clams usually mature as males first.

claims.text: The maximum lifespan of giant clams is not known. The oldest reliably aged one was a Tridacna gigas of 63 years, and growth rings put a 93 cm T. gigas at about 60 years old.
claims.evidenceNote: Status review section 2.3 (citing Lucas 1994 and Watanabe et al. 2004). Popular sources (Wikipedia, Great Barrier Reef Foundation) say up to or over 100 years, but give no aged specimen, so that figure is not used.

claims.text: Giant clams have 75 known predators, mostly bottom-dwellers. Triggerfish, wrasse and pufferfish bite the mantle or foot; crabs, snails and mantis shrimp chip, drill or crush small shells. In Palau one hermit crab crushed 26 juvenile T. gigas 20-30 mm long. Risk falls as clams grow, and adults are relatively immune.
claims.evidenceNote: Status review section 3.3.2 (giant clams generally, citing Neo et al. 2015 and Heslinga et al. 1984); the hermit-crab example is T. gigas-specific.

claims.text: Decades of intense, unregulated harvest for meat and shells have driven Tridacna gigas to very low numbers in much of its range; harvest is the main threat. Large adults are taken most because they are worth most.
claims.evidenceNote: NOAA's species page names overharvest as the primary threat; Wikipedia adds that mainly large adults are killed.

claims.text: Hot water can make giant clams bleach, expelling the algae that feed them. In 1997-98, about 8,000 of 9,000 surveyed T. gigas on the central Great Barrier Reef bleached to some degree. In Thailand in 2010, two-thirds of bleached T. squamosa died.
claims.evidenceNote: Status review section 3.5.1. Deaths are documented for T. squamosa; for T. gigas the report documents bleaching, not a death rate.

claims.text: Shells of long-dead giant clams can lie buried in the reef. In the South China Sea, boats used their propellers to dig up reef to reach these old shells for carving, destroying about 160 km² of reef together with island-building.
claims.evidenceNote: Status review section 3.1.3 ('Tanmen destructive shell harvesting'). The 160 km² figure covers clam dredging and island-building together.

claims.text: All giant clams are listed in CITES Appendix II (T. gigas since 1983), so international trade needs permits. In 2024 NOAA proposed listing T. gigas as endangered under the US Endangered Species Act, and the IUCN Red List assessed it as Critically Endangered. Australia has never allowed it to be collected from the wild.
claims.evidenceNote: CITES and ESA from NOAA (species page and status review section 3.4.2). The IUCN category (Critically Endangered, A2acd, 2024) was read from the WoRMS attribute record, not the IUCN site. ADW and the Great Barrier Reef Foundation still show the older 'Vulnerable' listing.

claims.text: Stories of giant clams trapping and drowning divers are myths: there are no authentic cases. Giant clams close slowly, and adult T. gigas cannot even shut their shells completely. Real injuries happen when people lift these very heavy clams.
claims.evidenceNote: University, conservation-charity and encyclopedia sources agree; Wikipedia adds that the slow adductor muscle and the need to push water out prevent trapping a person.

claims.text: The West Indian fuzzy chiton is Acanthopleura granulata (Gmelin, 1791), an accepted species in the World Register of Marine Species (AphiaID 386270), family Chitonidae, class Polyplacophora.
claims.evidenceNote: Authority and status read from the WoRMS REST record; the common name is from Wikipedia and Varney et al. (2021).

claims.text: SeaLifeBase gives a maximum length of 10 cm for Acanthopleura granulata; Wikipedia says it grows to about 7 cm.
claims.evidenceNote: 10 cm = 100 mm (maximum body length); 7 cm = 70 mm. Neither is a measured size distribution, so no typical range is given.

claims.text: Found in the tropical western Atlantic from southern Florida to Mexico, south to Panama and through the West Indies. It lives on rocks very high in the intertidal and spray zone of open rocky shores, where its colour and texture blend with the rock.
claims.evidenceNote: Range from Wikipedia (citing Malacolog) and SeaLifeBase ('Western Central Atlantic'), consistent with WoRMS distribution records and GBIF museum specimens (Bahamas 178, Cuba 100, Puerto Rico 48, Jamaica 48). Varney et al. collected their specimen in the Florida Keys.

claims.text: An intertidal animal: recorded from 0 to 1 m depth, on rocky shores up into the spray zone.
claims.evidenceNote: Depth range from SeaLifeBase; Schill et al. describe it as inhabiting the rocky intertidal shoreline.

claims.text: Eight thick, heavy shell plates, made only of aragonite, are surrounded by a girdle that is densely spiky and usually has a few black bands. In adults the plates are almost always heavily eroded; uneroded plates are granular. Tiny eyes and sensory pores (aesthetes) dot the plates.
claims.evidenceNote: Aragonite plates, eyes and aesthete pores from Varney et al. (peer-reviewed, with photographs of A. granulata); girdle and erosion from Wikipedia (citing Abbott and Warmke & Abbott).

claims.text: Hundreds of tiny eyes (ocelli) are set into the shell plates. Each has a pigment layer, a retina and a lens made of aragonite, the first aragonite lenses ever found. They work as small camera eyes with a resolution of about 9-12 degrees, in air and in water: chitons reacted to a dark circle appearing overhead but not to the light simply dimming.
claims.evidenceNote: From the abstract of Speiser et al. (2011), which studied A. granulata; Varney et al. show the eyes and aesthete pores in A. granulata plates.

claims.text: It grazes algae by scraping rock with its radula, whose teeth are capped with magnetite so they do not quickly dull; chitons make new rows of teeth within days. Wikipedia says its foraging is limited to night-time low tides, and a study of this species notes that tropical chitons limit daytime heat stress by staying in rocky microhabitats.
claims.evidenceNote: Radula and teeth from Varney et al. and UCMP (chitons generally). The night-time low-tide foraging comes only from Wikipedia, whose cited study (Focardi & Chelazzi 1990) could not be read, hence moderate.

claims.text: Chitons creep on a muscular foot and can cling to rock very powerfully, like a limpet; SeaLifeBase says this species adheres to rocks with great force. Because the shell is eight jointed plates, a chiton can bend over uneven rock and roll into a protective ball if it is knocked loose.
claims.evidenceNote: Rolling into a ball and the limpet comparison are stated for chitons generally (Wikipedia); the species-specific adhesion note is from SeaLifeBase.

claims.text: Acanthopleura granulata is a broadcast spawner. As in most chitons, males and females are separate: males release sperm into the water and females release eggs, which are fertilised in the water.
claims.evidenceNote: Broadcast spawning in A. granulata is stated by Varney et al. (citing Glynn 1970); separate sexes and external fertilisation are described for chitons generally by UCMP and Wikipedia.

claims.text: Chiton eggs usually hatch into a free-swimming trochophore larva that lives on its yolk and soon develops directly into a young chiton; unlike most molluscs there is no veliger stage. No larval duration was found for A. granulata.
claims.evidenceNote: Class-level statement; SeaLifeBase gives the same life cycle (lecithotrophic planktonic trochophore, no veliger) on the species page. UCMP describes the trochophore as 'soon' developing into a juvenile but gives no number of days.

claims.text: Animals that eat chitons include seagulls, sea stars, crabs, lobsters, fish and people. In countries that were part of the British West Indies, A. granulata and other intertidal chitons are called 'curb'; the foot is eaten and also used as fishing bait.
claims.evidenceNote: The predator list is for chitons generally; no species-specific predator study was read. The 'curb' use is from the species article.

claims.text: When a chiton dies, the girdle no longer holds the eight plates together, so they come apart. Single plates, sometimes called butterfly shells, may wash up in beach drift.
claims.evidenceNote: Stated for chitons generally.

claims.text: Acanthopleura granulata has not been evaluated for the IUCN Red List and is not assessed under CITES.
claims.evidenceNote: SeaLifeBase lists IUCN (version 2025-2), CITES and CMS status as 'Not Evaluated'. Local harvesting rules were not researched.

claims.text: The common tusk shell is Antalis vulgaris (da Costa, 1778), an accepted species in the World Register of Marine Species (AphiaID 196380), family Dentaliidae, class Scaphopoda.
claims.evidenceNote: Authority and status read from the WoRMS REST record; DORIS gives the same WoRMS number and family.

claims.text: The shell is 3 to 6 cm long and up to about 6 mm wide at the wide end. WoRMS records a maximum length of 60 mm.
claims.evidenceNote: 3-6 cm = 30-60 mm, from DORIS and Wikipedia; the 60 mm maximum is a WoRMS attribute citing two British identification guides.

claims.text: Lives from south-western Britain to the western Mediterranean, on sandy and detrital (shell-gravel) bottoms of the continental shelf. WoRMS records also include Ireland, Atlantic and Mediterranean Spain, Tunisia, the Aegean and the Sea of Marmara.
claims.evidenceNote: DORIS gives the range and 'sandy and detrital bottoms of the continental shelf'; SeaLifeBase gives 'Eastern Atlantic; Mediterranean'. The WoRMS distribution list is read directly from its REST endpoint.

claims.text: Recorded from about 5 to 1,000 m deep; DORIS says from the first few metres down to very great depths.
claims.evidenceNote: SeaLifeBase gives 5-1000 m, citing Steiner & Kabat (2004); Wikipedia gives the same range.

claims.text: A slightly curved, elephant-tusk-shaped tube open at both ends. It is opaque white, with many fine lengthwise ridges toward the narrow end, which is often stained brown (orange to black), and a few fine growth lines across the shell.
claims.evidenceNote: Description translated from DORIS; Wikipedia agrees on the white colour and lengthwise striations.

claims.text: A tusk shell lives buried head-down in sand or mud: the wide end, with the head and digging foot, points down, and only the narrow end reaches up into the water for water exchange and waste. To dig, it pushes out its foot and spreads the tip to anchor, then pulls itself along.
claims.evidenceNote: DORIS describes A. vulgaris living buried by its wider end; the anchoring foot and narrow end in the water are described for scaphopods generally by UCMP and Wikipedia.

claims.text: Its head carries many thread-like, club-tipped tentacles (captacula) that probe the sediment and carry food, mainly foraminifera and other tiny bottom-living organisms, to the mouth, where a large radula grinds it.
claims.evidenceNote: DORIS states the club-shaped captacula and foraminifera diet for A. vulgaris; UCMP and Wikipedia describe the radula for scaphopods generally.

claims.text: Tusk shells have no gills. Water enters through the narrow top end and cilia move it along the mantle, whose surface absorbs oxygen. When oxygen runs low, the water is pushed back out of the same top opening by muscle action, about every 10 to 12 minutes.
claims.evidenceNote: Class-level statement ('family' scope used for the wider group). The 10-12 minute interval is from Wikipedia only.

claims.text: Sexes are separate and the gametes are released into the water. The egg hatches into a free-swimming trochophore that becomes a shelled veliger larva, which settles on the bottom and grows into a miniature adult. No larval duration was found for A. vulgaris.
claims.evidenceNote: DORIS and Wikipedia describe external fertilisation; SeaLifeBase's class-level note says fertilisation occurs in the mantle cavity, so the place of fertilisation is not settled here. The trochophore-then-veliger sequence is in SeaLifeBase, UCMP and Wikipedia.

claims.text: Tusk shells are rarely seen alive by divers. More often one finds piles of empty shells on the seabed, and shells also wash up along the strandline.
claims.evidenceNote: Translated from DORIS ('Divers biologie').

claims.text: Empty tusk shells are often collected and, in some countries, still made into jewellery. Antalis vulgaris has not been evaluated for the IUCN Red List, and a European seabed index (AMBI) rates it as very sensitive to disturbance.
claims.evidenceNote: Jewellery use from DORIS; IUCN status from SeaLifeBase; AMBI group from the WoRMS attribute record (Borja et al. 2000). No collecting rules specific to this species were found.

claims.text: Neopilina galatheae Lemche, 1957 is an accepted species in the World Register of Marine Species (AphiaID 343689), family Neopilinidae, class Monoplacophora. Henning Lemche described it in Nature in February 1957.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS REST record read directly; only the Nature landing page (title, author, date) was accessible.

claims.text: The first living monoplacophoran was found on 6 May 1952 by the Danish Galathea deep-sea expedition: a trawl at 3,570 m off Costa Rica brought up 10 animals and three empty shells. The class had been thought extinct since the Palaeozoic, about 375 million years, so Neopilina was called a living fossil.
claims.evidenceNote: Date, depth and catch from the station data in Lemche & Wingstrand (station 716, 9°23'N 89°32'W). '375 million years' and 'living fossils' are from Chen (2024); Stöger et al. (2016) and Giribet et al. (2006) confirm the 1952 Galathea discovery.

claims.text: The 1952 shells measured 25 to 37 mm long: the largest 37 × 35 × 13 mm and the type specimen 33 × 30 × 10 mm. The shell is very thin, mostly under 0.2 mm.
claims.evidenceNote: Measured by Lemche & Wingstrand on the type material (length × width × height).

claims.text: Recorded from the deep eastern Pacific: first trawled at 3,570 m off Costa Rica on dark, muddy clay; later from the slope of the Cedros Trench off Mexico; and in 2023 at 2,460 m on the Galápagos Spreading Center, where one sat on hard basalt lava, about 1,000 km south-east of earlier records.
claims.evidenceNote: Earlier records were trawled from sand and mud (Chen 2024). The Mexican record is cited from its title only. WoRMS distribution lists the East Pacific and Costa Rica. Wikipedia also mentions Chile, which was not verified here.

claims.text: A single thin, almost circular, cap-shaped shell, with its apex near the front edge and slightly coiled. It is dull brown, darkening to almost black toward the apex and pale straw-brown near the edge, with fine growth lines crossed by 30 to 60 faint radial ribs. The surface is often corroded.
claims.evidenceNote: From the 'Shell and pallial fold' section of the anatomical monograph.

claims.text: Under the shell is a round central foot with five pairs of gills spaced along each side, kidneys (nephridia) repeated in series, and eight sets of paired foot-retractor muscles. This repetition of organs surprised zoologists when it was described.
claims.evidenceNote: Five gill pairs and the nephridial openings from Lemche & Wingstrand; the repeated gills, nephridia and eight sets of retractor muscles, and the zoological 'shock', from the Giribet et al. abstract.

claims.text: The guts of the 1952 animals held many radiolarians, scattered diatoms and much undefined detritus, so their describers concluded that Neopilina is a deposit feeder, probably gathering food with the tentacle tufts behind the mouth and a ciliated fold (velum) in front of it.
claims.evidenceNote: Gut contents and conclusion from Lemche & Wingstrand, who add that it is impossible to say exactly how these organs work. Chen (2024) saw no feeding trails near the 2023 animal.

claims.text: How Neopilina galatheae develops and how long it lives are unknown. No developmental studies have been done on any monoplacophoran, and this species was not collected again between 1959 and 2023. One 1952 specimen still carried a tiny coiled larval shell at its tip.
claims.evidenceNote: A sourced statement of ignorance: UCMP says no developmental studies have been done; Chen (2024) says the 2023 animal was the first collected since 1959; Lemche & Wingstrand describe the larval shell. No lifespan or larval duration was found in any source.

claims.text: A natural pearl forms when a parasite, organic matter or an injury carries cells of the mantle's outer layer into the soft body. They form a pocket, the pearl sac, which coats the intruder with calcium carbonate and the protein conchiolin.
claims.evidenceNote: The encyclopedia describes the pearl sac and the usual triggers; it says the process is 'thought' to work this way.

claims.text: Despite the common belief, a grain of sand is rarely what starts a pearl.
claims.evidenceNote: Stated directly in the encyclopedia article.

claims.text: Like the shell, a pearl is calcium carbonate laid down in concentric layers, and the pearl sac grows by cell division as the pearl grows. An X-ray of a natural pearl shows a series of concentric growth rings.
claims.evidenceNote: The rings drawn in the cut pearl are far wider and fewer than the real layers, so they can be seen.

claims.text: All shelled molluscs can make some kind of pearl, but most are not gems. The lustrous nacreous pearls come mainly from pearl oysters and freshwater mussels.
claims.evidenceNote: Stated in the encyclopedia article.

claims.text: Giant clam pearls are non-nacreous: porcelain-like, without nacre's rainbow sheen. They are built of crossed aragonite lamellae, which show a 'flame structure' and sometimes a silky shimmer.
claims.evidenceNote: GIA studied 37 pearls from the giant clam family (Tridacnidae), mainly Tridacna gigas, T. maxima and T. squamosa.

claims.text: Most giant clam pearls studied are symmetrical around one axis and show spiral patterns at their ends, which suggests they turn as they grow.
claims.evidenceNote: 35 of the 37 pearls had cylindrical symmetry; GIA reads this as suggesting rotation, not proving it.

claims.text: Tridacna gigas has yielded flame-structure pearls weighing several tens of carats, and very large concretions such as the Pearl of Allah, a blister pearl that grew against the shell and was cut from it.
claims.evidenceNote: One carat is 0.2 g, so several tens of carats is several grams. The drawn sizes of loose pearls are illustrative, not measurements.

claims.text: The Pearl of Lao Tzu (also called the Pearl of Allah), from a giant clam off Palawan in the Philippines, measures 24 cm across and weighs 6.4 kg.
claims.evidenceNote: Its early history rests on one owner's accounts, which the encyclopedia treats as embellished; the size and weight are not disputed. GIA gives about 6.37 kg.

claims.text: How long a giant clam pearl takes to grow was not found in the sources reviewed, so the slider shows sizes along the way, not ages.
claims.evidenceNote: A limit of this demo rather than a fact about the animal.

claims.text: Tropical cowries produce many swimming veliger larvae from each egg capsule. In tiger cowries kept in the lab, a capsule held about 740 larvae on average, and a brood hatched over 1 to 3 days, with 90% of the larvae released overnight on the final day.
claims.evidenceNote: Counts and hatching timing are from captive tiger cowries (table 1 and section 3.1.1); 'numerous planktotrophic veligers per capsule' is stated for tropical cowries in general. How closely siblings stay together once in the open sea is not measured.

claims.text: In the wild, a brooding tiger cowrie was found in a crevice among coral rubble, sitting on its purplish-red egg mass. In the lab the capsules were glued in up to five layers to a hard surface and kept covered by the mother's foot until they hatched.
claims.evidenceNote: The field record is a single sighting on an intertidal reef in Singapore; the layering and covering foot are from captive brooders.

claims.text: Most cowries brood their eggs: the female glues her egg capsules to a hard surface and covers the egg mass with her foot until the larvae hatch.
claims.evidenceNote: Stated for cowries in general in the study's introduction; not observed for the money cowrie itself.

claims.text: Cone snails glue each egg capsule by an adhesive base to a hard surface, usually the underside of a rock or dead coral. In Hawaii, clusters held 1 to 68 capsules, each with 80 to about 10,000 eggs, and females were often found under the same rock.
claims.evidenceNote: Field collections of nine Hawaiian Conus species; Conus textile was not among them.

claims.text: Queen conch generally lay their egg masses in clean coral sand with little organic matter. The mass is one long tube folded and stuck into a compact clump, and sand grains stuck to it camouflage it.
claims.evidenceNote: A NOAA review summarising field studies (Randall 1964; D'Asaro 1965).

claims.text: Nautilus eggs have never been seen in the wild. In aquariums the female lays them in crevices or between corals, and they hatch after 9 to 15 months, depending on water temperature.
claims.evidenceNote: From captive breeding only; where wild nautilus lay their eggs is unknown.

claims.text: Newly hatched tiger cowrie veligers have translucent shells 200–242 micrometres long, tinged purple-red at the first whorl, a two-lobed velum, paired eyespots, a rudimentary foot and an operculum. Shells have not yet completed their first whorl. The velum expands into four distinctly bifurcated arms by 14 days after hatching.
claims.evidenceNote: Section 3.1.2 and microscopy figures 3–4, read directly. The money cowrie model borrows this general cowrie form, not a measured species-specific reconstruction. Displayed age progression is illustrative, not a calendar.
